questions.stem: A department recorded 6, 9, 7, 8, and 10 first-aid cases during five equal reporting periods. What is the arithmetic mean?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Add the five observations and divide by five: (6 + 9 + 7 + 8 + 10) / 5 = 40 / 5 = 8.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Seven is below the sum divided by the number of observations.
A result of 7.5 would follow from an incorrect total or divisor.
Ten is the maximum observation, not the arithmetic mean.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, descriptive statistics and mean, pp. 408-409
questions.formula: Mean = sum of observations / number of observations

questions.stem: Corrective-action closure times were 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, and 27 days. Which value is the median and why is it useful here?
options: 3 days; the median is always the second observation after sorting.
5 days; the median equals the most frequent upper-half observation.
7.5 days; the median is calculated by averaging all observations.
4 days; the median is the middle of the ordered data.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: With six ordered observations, the median is the average of the third and fourth values: (4 + 4) / 2 = 4. It is robust to the extreme 27-day value.
incorrectOptionExplanations: For six observations, the middle lies between the third and fourth values, not at the second value.
Five is an observed value but not the midpoint of the ordered data set.
Averaging all observations produces the mean, not the median.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, median and central tendency, pp. 409-411
questions.formula: Median for even n = average of the two middle ordered observations

questions.stem: A sample contains the values 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12. What is the sample standard deviation, rounded to two decimals?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The mean is 8. Squared deviations total 40. For a sample, divide by n - 1: 40 / 4 = 10, then take the square root: s = 3.16.
incorrectOptionExplanations: 2.83 is the population standard deviation obtained by dividing by n rather than n - 1.
Four is the number of degrees of freedom, not the standard deviation.
Ten is the sample variance before taking the square root.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, variance and standard deviation, pp. 409-411

questions.stem: A safety metric has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 6. What is the z-score for an observed value of 68?
incorrectOptionExplanations: A z-score of 2.0 would correspond to a value 12 units above the mean.
Eight is not obtained by standardizing the difference from the mean.
Eighteen is the raw difference, not the difference expressed in standard-deviation units.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: Annual exposure measurements are approximately normal with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 10. Approximately what proportion exceeds 120?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A value of 120 is two standard deviations above the mean. The upper-tail probability beyond z = 2.00 is approximately 0.0228, or 2.3%.
incorrectOptionExplanations: About 15.9% is the upper-tail probability above one standard deviation, not two.
Half the observations exceed the mean of 100, not a point two standard deviations above it.
About 97.7% is the cumulative proportion below 120, not the proportion above it.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, normal distribution and z-score application, pp. 411-412 and 420-422
questions.formula: z = (X - mean) / standard deviation; upper tail = 1 - Phi(z)

questions.concept: Expected frequency from a sample proportion
questions.stem: A random sample found 8 defective units among 400 inspected. At the same observed defect rate, how many defective units would be expected in a lot of 2,500?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The observed defect proportion is 8 / 400 = 0.02. Applying 2% to 2,500 gives 0.02 × 2,500 = 50.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Twenty would represent only 0.8% of the larger lot.
Eighty would represent 3.2%, exceeding the observed sample rate.
One hundred twenty-five would represent 5%, not the observed 2%.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, probability and proportional estimation examples, pp. 417-420
questions.formula: Expected count = sample proportion × target population

questions.stem: An analysis finds a Pearson correlation of -0.88 between preventive-maintenance completion and unplanned equipment failures. What is the best interpretation?
options: A strong inverse linear association exists, but correlation alone does not establish causation.
The variables have no meaningful relationship because the coefficient is negative.
Maintenance completion explains exactly 88% of all equipment failures and proves causation.
The calculation is invalid because a correlation coefficient cannot be less than zero.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A coefficient near -1 indicates a strong negative linear association: higher maintenance completion tends to accompany fewer failures. Correlation does not, by itself, demonstrate causation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The sign indicates direction, not absence of association; the magnitude 0.88 is strong.
The coefficient itself is not the percentage explained, and observational correlation does not prove causation.
Valid Pearson coefficients range from -1 to +1, so negative values are expected for inverse relationships.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, Pearson correlation coefficient, pp. 412-415

questions.stem: Two continuous safety variables have a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.80. What is the coefficient of determination?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.80² = 0.64. It represents the proportion of variation associated with the fitted linear relationship, subject to the study design and assumptions.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Subtracting r from 1 does not calculate the coefficient of determination.
The correlation coefficient and coefficient of determination are different measures.
Doubling r is not meaningful and produces an impossible proportion above 100%.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, coefficient of determination and correlation, pp. 422-425

questions.stem: Three independent components in a series safety system have reliabilities of 0.98, 0.95, and 0.97. What is the system reliability?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Every component must work in a series system, so multiply the component reliabilities: 0.98 × 0.95 × 0.97 = 0.90307.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Averaging or choosing a middle component does not represent the requirement that all components succeed.
Series reliability is lower than each individual reliability, not nearly perfect for these values.
Adding reliabilities produces a value above 1 and is not a valid probability.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, system and series reliability, pp. 424-425

questions.stem: Two independent redundant components operate in parallel. Their reliabilities are 0.90 and 0.80, and the system succeeds if either component works. What is system reliability?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Both components must fail for the parallel system to fail. Failure probability is (0.10)(0.20) = 0.02, so reliability is 1 - 0.02 = 0.98.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Multiplying the component reliabilities calculates joint success, not the reliability of an either-can-succeed parallel system.
A simple average ignores the redundancy logic and the probability of both components failing.
Adding probabilities without accounting for overlap yields an impossible value above 1.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A switch is operated three times per day and records one failure after eight years of operation. Using 365 days per year, what is the observed failure rate per operation?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Total operations = 3 × 365 × 8 = 8,760. The observed rate is 1 / 8,760 = 0.000114, or 1.14 × 10^-4 per operation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This result fails to divide by the three daily operations correctly.
This rate is much too large and does not use the total number of operating cycles.
This is the number of operations, not failures per operation.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, component reliability and probability of failure, pp. 422-425
questions.formula: Observed failure rate = number of failures / number of operations

questions.stem: A safety analyst wants to test whether training completion status (completed/not completed) is associated with incident involvement (yes/no). Which statistical test is most appropriate for the resulting count table?
options: A paired t test comparing two measurements from the same continuous variable.
A chi-square test of association using the categorical count table.
A Pearson correlation calculated from the four cell labels rather than their counts.
A z-score for one employee selected from the table.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Both variables are categorical, and the data are frequencies in a contingency table. A chi-square test evaluates whether the observed counts differ from counts expected under independence.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A paired t test is used for paired continuous measurements and does not match a two-by-two frequency table.
Pearson correlation is not calculated from category labels and is not the standard test for association in this table.
A single z-score standardizes one value and does not test association between two categorical variables.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 15, chi-square statistic and degrees of freedom, pp. 416-417
